title: Using Mini Whiteboards to Optimise Ratio and Make Thinking Visible in GCSE Economics d-make-thinking-visible-in-gcse-economics/
author: Mason Davies
summary: Mason Davies details the start-of-lesson mini-whiteboard (MWB) routine he built for his GCSE Economics class as part of a professional-learning project on 'ratio' -- how many students are thinking at any given moment, and how hard. He walks through how the routine was built incrementally over several weeks, from establishing the basic habit of picking up a whiteboard and pen and working in silence, through the 'hover your boards... show me' reveal step, to the final and most important stage: explicitly explaining to students why each element matters. Davies reports the routine gave him a clearer picture of both whole-class and individual understanding, closer to 100% participation ratio, and better insight into curriculum sequencing gaps, while giving students a clearer sense of their own understanding and material for later revision flashcards.
points: Davies frames mini-whiteboards as a tool for building 'ratio' -- maximising both how many students are thinking and how hard they're thinking -- not just a display device.
He built the routine incrementally over weeks, praising specific compliant behaviour by name at each stage rather than assuming the routine would form itself.
The final and 'probably the most important' step is explaining the why behind each element of the routine, which he says drove genuine student buy-in.
He reports concrete effects: near-100% participation ratio, clearer visibility into individual and whole-class misconceptions, and better data on whether the curriculum itself is sequenced well.
quotes: In short, it means how many students are thinking at one time, and how hard each of them is thinking. As a group, we discussed how MWBs are also a great tool for building ratio in our lessons.
Now I know what you might be thinking, 'my, there are quite a few steps in that routine'. Rome wasn't built in a day, and neither was this routine.
The final step in establishing the routine, and I think probably the most important, is explaining the ‘why’ to the students.

It has given me a better picture of whole class understanding and misconceptions – making thinking more visible than before. It has ensured that I have 100% participation ratio (at least for this phase of the lesson!)
Misconceptions are less likely to be embedded leading to a greater chance of success and subsequent motivation.
